tldr: We built 360CityArena, a benchmark measuring the navigation and spatial reasoning capabilities of AI agents in an ultra-realistic urban environment of Akihabara reconstructed from real-world 360-degree videos. Even state-of-the-art LMM agents achieved at best 17.1% accuracy compared to 77.3% for humans, revealing that real-world urban exploration remains a massive hurdle.
hero_caption: Conceptual diagram of 360CityArena. By stitching together 360-degree videos captured on the streets of Akihabara, it recreates a realistic urban environment bustling with pedestrians and vehicles. Agents tackle practical tasks such as path guidance and landmark search relying on visual observations and maps.
overview:
Expectations are rising for Embodied AI that can observe its surroundings and act autonomously to help lost pedestrians or guide visually impaired individuals on city streets. However, existing evaluation simulators either look overly synthetic and lack complexity, or rely on static panorama cutouts without dynamic elements like pedestrians, leaving a substantial gap from real-world urban navigation.

To address this, the authors developed 360CityArena, an ultra-realistic and dynamic virtual urban environment reconstructed as a pose graph from 602 360-degree video segments of Akihabara, Tokyo. It covers a vast area measuring 750m north-south by 650m east-west across 85 streets, offering 175 human-crafted tasks spanning three categories: Environment Understanding, Path Reasoning, and Spatial Reasoning.

Using this environment, the authors evaluated state-of-the-art large multimodal models (LMMs) as agents, including GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and InternVL. While human participants with local experience easily solved 77.3% of the tasks on average, the best-performing model, Gemini 2.5 Flash, achieved a remarkably low score of just 17.1%.

Further failure analysis revealed distinct bottlenecks across models—such as exploratory stagnation versus low-level action execution failures—as well as a map-view misalignment issue where providing a localization map does not necessarily improve performance. 360CityArena serves as an exceptionally challenging and practical testbed for developing AI that can truly operate in real cities.
contributions: Constructed 360CityArena, an ultra-realistic urban exploration benchmark reconstructing the streetscapes of Akihabara with dynamic pedestrians and vehicles from a 360-degree video pose graph.
Manually designed and systematized 175 tasks across three categories and seven sub-tasks (Environment Understanding, Path Reasoning, and Spatial Reasoning) with difficulty levels (Easy/Medium/Hard).
Evaluated agents using state-of-the-art proprietary and open-source LMMs, demonstrating an overwhelming performance gap between humans (77.3%) and leading LMMs (17.1% with Gemini 2.5 Flash).

Comprehensively analyzed the differences between image-based and text-based goal specifications, the impact of localization map information on reasoning, and detailed model-specific failure modes (action, exploration, perception, etc.).

sections.heading: Why Have AI Walk Through an Ultra-Realistic Akihabara?
sections.summary: Evaluating autonomous agents for the real world requires benchmarks that capture dynamic and complex urban environments. This work introduces 360CityArena, which reconstructs Akihabara from 360-degree videos to rigorously evaluate the current capabilities of LMM agents.
sections.details:
Developing AI assistants capable of guiding visually impaired people or offering directions requires evaluating agents in environments that capture the full complexity of city streets. However, existing 3D simulators suffer from synthetic visual artifacts, while Google Street View-based environments lack dynamic elements like pedestrians and cars and do not support continuous visual transitions. Furthermore, top-down navigation or route planning on 2D maps fails to evaluate down-to-earth pedestrian exploration skills.

To bridge this gap, this paper introduces 360CityArena, a benchmark set in Akihabara, Tokyo. Reconstructed as a pose graph—a network representing camera positions and connectivity—from 360-degree videos, it spans 85 streets covering roughly 750m north-south and 650m east-west. Akihabara features narrow sidewalks, crowded signboards, and diverse commercial facilities, making it an urban environment with exceptionally rich visual and spatial information.

The benchmark consists of three categories and seven sub-tasks, totaling 175 human-crafted tasks organized by difficulty. Experimental results show that modern LMM agents fall far short of human performance, highlighting numerous challenges remaining before practical deployment.

captions.F2: Examples of the three task categories and seven sub-tasks in 360CityArena. It covers key capabilities required for urban exploration, including localization, landmark search with language and image, map navigation, VLN, object counting, and relational spatial reasoning between landmarks.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Embodied AI and Urban Simulators
sections.summary: Embodied navigation has shifted from simple indoor scenes to large-scale outdoor spaces. However, conventional computer graphics and street-view setups have struggled to combine visual realism with dynamic elements.
sections.details:
Embodied agents are AIs that interpret their surroundings via cameras and sensors to execute actions following language instructions. While research has accelerated with advances in LMMs, real-robot experiments remain costly and hard to reproduce, leading to the widespread adoption of simulation environments.

Early simulators focused primarily on indoor spaces, but due to their simple scale and floor plans, research has expanded outdoors. Outdoor tasks include PointGoal (reaching coordinate targets), ImageGoal (navigating to reference images), ObjectGoal (finding language-specified objects), and Vision-Language Navigation (VLN, following natural language route directions). Nonetheless, many benchmarks evaluate pathfinding strictly on maps or from aerial perspectives, leaving a gap with ground-level pedestrian exploration.

Methods for building real-world simulations have included 3D reconstruction via NeRF or 3D Gaussian Splatting, conventional CG simulators, and Google Street View. However, NeRF-based approaches tend to be restricted to static scenes, CG lacks visual realism, and Street View is discrete without moving people or vehicles. This paper leverages video-based virtual world techniques to achieve an environment that includes dynamic pedestrians and cars while supporting continuous exploration.

sections.heading: Inside 360CityArena: Akihabara's Streetscape and Task Design
sections.summary: Built on a pose graph of 602 Akihabara 360-degree video segments, the benchmark contains seven sub-tasks totaling 175 instances. Tasks were crafted by annotators familiar with the area and evaluated using four objective metrics.
sections.details:
The design and tasks of 360CityArena are detailed as follows:

- 3.1 Akihabara Virtual Environment
The environment is built from 602 360-degree video segments. Projected onto spheres within Unity, it forms a single connected pose graph with 193 nodes and 305 edges (average out-degree of 3.16). Agents traverse viewpoints and select intersections along this graph. Covering 750m north-south by 650m east-west around Akihabara Station, each street was captured bidirectionally to reflect differences in appearance depending on the walking direction.

- 3.2 Task Categories
The benchmark comprises three main categories and seven sub-tasks (25 questions each):
1. Environment Understanding: Localization (identifying one's position on a 5×5 grid), Landmark Search with Language, and Landmark Search with Image.
2. Path Reasoning: Map Navigation (reaching goals using map information) and Vision-Language Navigation (VLN, following multi-step natural language instructions).
3. Spatial Reasoning: Relational Spatial Reasoning (inferring cardinal directions relative to reference landmarks) and Object Count (tallying target objects within a specified area).

- 3.3 Task Construction
Tasks were crafted directly in Unity by eight annotators who had visited Akihabara, ensuring all questions are solvable. Each task is categorized as Easy, Medium, or Hard based on travel distance, instruction ambiguity, and landmark visibility.

- 3.4 Evaluation Protocol
Four metrics are utilized depending on task characteristics. Localization uses exact match (exact_match); Relational Spatial Reasoning uses semantic matching powered by GPT-5 (fuzzy_match, kappa coefficient of 0.937 with human judgments); navigational tasks use coordinate matching based on Euclidean distance to the goal (coordinate_match, 10m default threshold, 20m for Map Navigation); and Object Count uses Mean Relative Accuracy (MRA) to continuously evaluate error magnitude.

captions.F3: The visual observation interface for an agent in 360CityArena. The agent can look around 360 degrees, move forward, and choose which path to take when reaching intersections or branching points (red arrows) to explore the city.

sections.heading: How Does an Agent Navigate the City?
sections.summary: We formulate urban exploration as a partially observable Markov decision process and deploy agents powered by recent proprietary and open-source LMMs. Agents maintain past reasoning in memory and select from seven discrete actions.
sections.details:
This study formulates agent-environment interaction as a partially observable sequential decision process $\mathcal{E}=(S, A, \Omega, T)$.

At each time step $t$, the agent receives a partial observation $o_t$ comprising the current visual image and a localization map image. It also maintains a Reflection Memory $M_t$ that summarizes past reasoning and observations. These inputs are fed into the prompt for LMM inference to determine the next action $a_t$. The action space $A$ consists of seven discrete actions: move forward, pitch view up/down, turn left/right, reset orientation, and submit answer. Branching selection actions are added when arriving at intersections.

Evaluated baseline models include commercial systems (GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash) and open-source models (Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct, InternVL3.5-8B, InternVL3.5-38B). Open-source models were evaluated across eight NVIDIA A100 (80GB) GPUs, with all tasks running on Unity 6 LTS.

sections.heading: Humans vs. AI: A Massive Gap and Uncovered Bottlenecks
sections.summary: While humans familiar with Akihabara reached 77.3% accuracy, the top-performing Gemini 2.5 Flash scored only 17.1%. In-depth error analysis revealed model-specific weaknesses and unexpected pitfalls of map information.
sections.details:
Key findings from the experiments include:

- Overwhelming Gap Between Humans and LMMs (Finding 1)
Human participants with local knowledge achieved an average success rate of 77.3%, reaching around 90% on Map Navigation, VLN, and Image Landmark Search. In contrast, the top-ranking LMM, Gemini 2.5 Flash, achieved only 17.1% (GPT-5 scored 15.8%), lagging far behind. Models fell particularly behind on Map Navigation, Object Count, and Relational Spatial Reasoning.

- Visual vs. Language Targets (Finding 2)
In landmark search, providing image goals yielded higher success rates across most models than language goals (e.g., GPT-5 achieved 16.0% with language vs. 48.0% with image). Concrete visual cues like building facades and signboard colors served as highly effective navigation guides.

- Performance Drop Across Difficulty Levels (Finding 3)
All models displayed clear performance drops as difficulty progressed from Easy to Medium and Hard, validating the benchmark's difficulty differentiation.

- The Adverse Effect of Map Information
Comparing agents with and without localization maps revealed that map access did not consistently boost performance. In fact, accuracy dropped for Language Landmark Search (24.0% to 16.0%) and Relational Reasoning (48.0% to 32.0%). This stems from the agent's inability to accurately ground 2D map coordinates with first-person 3D visual perspectives.

- Model-Specific Failure Patterns
Categorizing failures into five types (Action, Grounding, Perception, Exploration, Planning) revealed that GPT-5 made few low-level action errors but suffered from exploratory stagnation—looping in place—in 55% of its failures. Conversely, Gemini 2.5 Flash and InternVL exhibited around 40% low-level action errors, highlighting fragility in low-level control and prompt adherence.

captions.F6: A failure example in Landmark Search with Language when looking for 'Jonathan\'s'. The agent misidentified a Hotto Motto sign as indicating the restaurant was on the upper floor, spending all remaining steps pitching its view up and down without moving until it hit the step limit.
captions.F7: A successful run for the same target (Jonathan's) when given an image goal. By identifying the blue-and-white facade at the building corner from the photo, the agent ignored the Hotto Motto shop, correctly proceeded to the intersection, and reached the destination.

sections.heading: Remaining Limitations and What Comes Next
sections.summary: Video-based motion constraints and coverage limited to a single district (Akihabara) are the main drawbacks. Future efforts will target freer navigation and multi-city expansion.
sections.details:
360CityArena has two primary limitations.

First, because it relies on pre-recorded 360-degree videos, agents can only move along the nodes of the captured video graph, preventing arbitrary 3D continuous movement or physical environmental interaction. Trajectory switching discontinuities accounted for 11.3% of the execution log, though analysis showed this rarely caused task failures directly. Still, enabling unconstrained locomotion and richer interactions is an essential future goal.

Second, the benchmark currently covers only one urban district, Akihabara, limiting evaluations of urban diversity and cross-city generalization. However, the framework of building pose graphs from 360-degree videos using GPS/SLAM and map alignment is generic, and expanding it to diverse cities worldwide is an exciting next step.

sections.heading: Paving the Way for Urban Embodied AI
sections.summary: We proposed 360CityArena, an ultra-realistic urban exploration benchmark, uncovering where cutting-edge LMMs currently stand. Evaluating models in near-real-world environments will accelerate the development of practical city assistant AI.
sections.details:
This paper introduced 360CityArena, an embodied navigation benchmark that faithfully reconstructs Akihabara from 360-degree videos. Comprehensive experiments with state-of-the-art LMM agents highlight the substantial hurdles that remain in real-world urban understanding and spatial reasoning.

The benchmark serves not only as an evaluation testbed, but also as a blueprint for generating training data in photorealistic virtual spaces. Providing an environment closely mirroring real streets will significantly contribute to realizing embodied AI that can naturally assist humans in daily urban life.

sections.heading: Appendix: Task Details and Agent Prompting
sections.summary: The appendix provides details on the 5×5 grid map for localization, agent prompt designs, and termination conditions.
sections.details:
The appendix elaborates on experimental protocols and prompting details.

Map data is cropped from OpenStreetMap. For the Localization task, a 5×5 grid map dividing Akihabara (Figure F8) is provided as reference, requiring the agent to predict its $(x, y)$ coordinate. Termination conditions preventing runaway behavior include exceeding 50 steps, repeating the same stationary action 20 consecutive times, or moving away from the goal for 5 consecutive steps.

The prompting architecture uses a three-tier design: a System Prompt defining reasoning procedures and action syntax; a Reflection Prompt updating past reasoning in text to maintain long-term memory; and a Task Prompt providing task-specific instructions. Landmarks, target images, and route instructions can be dynamically swapped, ensuring high reproducibility across benchmarks.

captions.F8: The 5×5 grid map presented to agents in the Localization task. The agent must infer which cell (x, y) it is standing in based on street-level visual observations of Akihabara.

takeaways: In real urban settings with dynamic pedestrians, cars, and dense signage—factors often missing from static or synthetic CG environments—LMM agents perform far below humans (77.3% human vs. 17.1% best LMM).
Visual targets yield higher search success than text descriptions, as concrete visual features like facade textures and signboard colors serve as powerful navigation cues.
Providing 2D localization maps does not guarantee performance gains; grounding 2D map coordinates with first-person 3D visual views remains a critical bottleneck for modern LMMs.

Failure patterns vary widely across models: GPT-5 struggles with exploratory stagnation (looping in place), while Gemini and open-source models stumble on low-level action control, indicating that distinct remedies are required for each.
limitations: Agent movement is restricted to the pre-recorded 360-degree video pose graph, preventing free exploration across arbitrary 3D continuous space or physical interactions like opening doors.
Evaluation is currently confined to a single district (Akihabara, Tokyo), leaving cross-city generalization across different urban layouts unverified.
